title: Iggy the Incredible Inventor

subtitle.text: It all started one Monday morning at school.
"It" was my idea—my first invention!
We were sitting in class, coloring maps.
I don't understand why our teacher, Mrs. Romano, makes us color maps.
She acts as if we are in first grade instead of fourth grade.
Does she really think we still like to color?
"Use bright colors!"
Mrs. Romano said, walking around the room.
I colored North America green.
I colored South America orange.I
colored Africa yellow. Then
I started working on Asia, which is a really big continent. My
hand was getting tired. I
stopped to give it a rest. My
friend Molly leaned toward me. "Psst,
Iggy!" she whispered. "My
hand hurts from coloring!" "So
does mine!" I said. "Quiet,
please!" said Mrs. Romano. "All
I want to hear is the sound of crayons moving across the paper." Mrs.
Romano wanted to hear the sound of crayons moving across the paper? I
was so tired of that sound! "Why
aren't there machines to do coloring?" I
thought suddenly. "Then
kids wouldn't have to work so hard." That
was when I got my idea—a truly incredible idea. It
could make me, Iggy, a famous inventor! I
told Molly about my idea on the way home from school. "Wow!"
said Molly. "If
your idea works, we'll never have to color by hand again!" Our
school is near the apartment building where Molly and I live. Our
apartments are both on the fifth floor. That
means we have to climb a lot of stairs every day. "Whew,
I wish our backpacks weren't so heavy!" I groaned. "Me
too," she agreed, panting hard. I
said good-bye to Molly and then went into my apartment. My
mom was on the telephone in the kitchen. She
waved to me as I walked by.
I went into my bedroom and dumped my heavy backpack on the floor.
One of its straps fell just over the chalk line on the floor.
My older brother, Tate, had drawn the line to divide our room into two sections.
"Hey, get your backpack off my side of the room!"
Tate ordered me.
"It's my room too!" I shot back.
"No arguing, boys!" called my mother from the kitchen.
I decided to go down to the fourth floor and see my friend Josh.
I wanted to get away from Tate.
Plus, I needed help with my invention.
I knocked on the door of his apartment, and Josh answered right away.
"Hi, Josh!" I said.
Josh invited me in.
"Do you know that toy that Sparky likes?" I blurted out.
Sparky is Josh's pet hamster.
"His seesaw?" Josh asked.
He walked over to Sparky's cage and lifted up the toy.
"Yes, that's it," I said.
"Can I borrow it?
I want to make one just like it."
"Why?" asked Josh.
"I have a brilliant idea!" I said.
"I'm going to invent an automatic coloring machine!
My hand will never get tired from coloring again."
Josh's eyes lit up.
"Cool," he said. "How will it work?"
"You'll see!" I told him.
"Let's show Sparky's seesaw to Mr. Calabria, the building superintendent.
He has a lot of wood downstairs."
We went down the steps to the building's basement.
Mr. Calabria was in his workroom surrounded by tools and wood scraps.
He smiled at us.
"Is your kitchen faucet leaking again, Iggy?" he asked.
I shook my head.
"Our faucet is working fine."
"Then do you have another problem?" he asked.
"He has something, Mr. Calabria!" Josh burst out.
"But it's not a problem—it's an amazing, incredible idea!"
Mr. Calabria helped Josh and me make three coloring machines.
Josh's little sister, Jenny, helped too.
So did their dog, Bunch.
He picked up all the pieces of wood we dropped on the floor.
"This is the best invention in the world!" Josh told me.
Josh always says things like that.
He's the best friend in the world.
"I sure hope these coloring machines work," said Jenny, sneezing.
Everything makes Jenny sneeze, especially wood scraps and dust.
Even Josh's hamster, Sparky, makes Jenny sneeze.
"I'm going to bring the coloring machines to school tomorrow," I said.
"Wait until the other kids see them!"
"You'll be the most famous kid in school!" said Josh.
"Ah-choo!" Jenny sneezed.
The next day I took my coloring machines to school with me.
Mrs. Romano was very impressed with my invention.
"What a creative idea, Iggy!" she said.
"Our hands will never get tired from coloring again!" said Jake.
"Even when we have to color Asia," said Ruby.
Everyone laughed, remembering how long it had taken to color Asia.
Molly, Ruby, and Evan volunteered to try out my new invention.
I showed them how to tape their crayons inside the round part of the machine.
"Move the machine around so the crayon colors," I explained.
"Let the machine do all the work!"
Evan started filling in North America with blue.
"This is really hard, Iggy,"
he said as he moved the automatic coloring machine around.
Ruby frowned. "It's even harder than coloring by hand!"
"Well, at least your hand doesn't get tired," I pointed out.
"Look, my crayon broke!" Ruby said with dismay.
"Mine did too!" said Evan.
Molly looked at me.
"Iggy, this is a brilliant invention," she said.
I grinned proudly. "Really?"
"Yes," said Molly. "But there's only one problem."
"What's that?" I asked.
"It doesn't work!" said Molly.
I hated to admit it.
But Molly was right.
That day when I got home from school, I felt really bad.
My coloring machine was a big failure.
I threw the machines in the back of my bedroom closet.
I didn't want to ever see them again.
"Mom! Iggy threw his invention junk in my half of the closet!" yelled Tate.
"Boys, please be quiet!" called Mom.
"I'm talking on the telephone!"
I lay down on my bed to think.
I wished I could think of a really wonderful new invention—one that actually worked.
There was a knock on the apartment door.
It was Molly.
"Iggy, Caswell has disappeared again!" she cried.
Caswell is Molly's little brother.
He loves to go exploring in our old apartment building.
He likes to look for hidden treasure, but sometimes he gets lost.
Once we found him in the basement.
Another time we found him on the roof.
I couldn't imagine who would hide a treasure on the roof!
Everyone helped look for Caswell, except for Mom, who was still on the phone.
"Caswell, where are you?" we called.
"Caswell, you come here right this minute!" ordered Molly.
"Ruff, ruff!" barked Bunch.
But there was no sign of Caswell.
"Caswell! Caswell, come back!" we shouted.
We looked in the basement and up on the roof.
We even looked in our tiny backyard, but all we saw was a cat.
She was wearing a bell around her neck that tinkled whenever she walked.
That was when I got my next brilliant idea!
It would help us find Caswell whenever he got lost.
It was the best idea I'd ever had.
But first we needed to find Caswell!
"Caswell!" Josh yelled.
"Where are you?" said Molly.
"He's got to be here somewhere," said Mrs. O'Donnell.
Everyone was still calling for Caswell.
All at once we heard a small, muffled voice.
"Here I am!" Caswell appeared from a dark space under the stairs.
He was completely covered with dust.
"Ah-choo!" Molly sneezed a few times.
"Look what I found under the stairs!" said Caswell.
He was clutching an old penny.
"Caswell, I am so glad to see you," cried Mrs. O'Donnell.
"When we couldn't find you, we were all very worried!"
"I found a treasure!"
said Caswell, proudly holding out his penny.
"You are my treasure!"
said Mrs. O'Donnell, hugging Caswell.
"He's a pest, that's what he is," said Molly.
But she was smiling as she ruffled her brother's hair.
"I'm glad we found you."
I couldn't wait to get back to my room to plan my new invention.
It was going to be great.
Caswell would never be lost again—at least not for long.
The first thing I needed was a bell.
Luckily, I knew just where to find one.
My mom keeps a box of Christmas tree ornaments in our coat closet.
One of the ornaments was a beautiful brass bell.
I went in the closet and opened the box.
I found lots of ornaments, including a colored glass ball and a gingerbread house.
At last I found the brass bell.
After that I got some string.
I tied the bell to the string and jingled it.
It made a nice loud ringing noise.
If we could get Caswell to wear the bell, he'd jingle wherever he went.
So we'd always be able to find him!
I decided to bring the bell to school tomorrow to show Molly and the other kids. Then
they would see that I was a really good inventor. By
this time I was getting really hungry. I
went into the kitchen to see what Mom was making for dinner. But
Mom was still talking on the phone! There
was nothing cooking on the stove. And
there were no good smells coming from the oven. "What's
the matter with Mom lately?" I wondered. "All
she does is talk on the phone." And
tonight it looked like she had forgotten to make dinner for Tate and me. I
was about to look for something to eat when I heard something strange. "I'll
have to rob a bank," my mom said into the phone. And
then she laughed! Oh
my gosh! My
mom works as a bank teller. But
that wouldn't turn her into a bank robber , would it?
I decided I'd better tell someone about it right away.
So I ran to Molly's apartment and knocked on the door.
When Molly answered, I could smell something really good coming from her kitchen.
It smelled like roast beef, which is my favorite food.
"Molly, my mom is planning to rob a bank!" I cried.
"What?" Molly blinked in surprise.
"What on earth are you talking about, Iggy?"
"I heard her on the telephone," I explained.
"She said she was going to rob a bank.
She even laughed about it!"
Molly stared at me.
"You know what?" she said.
"What?" I said.
I was hoping Molly would know how to stop my mother from robbing a bank.
Molly shook her head.
"You like to invent things, Iggy.
And now you're inventing stories!"
"Maybe Molly was right," I thought when I got home.
Maybe I was inventing stories.
Still I knew what I had heard.
My mom had clearly said, " I'll have to rob a
bank ." I didn't
invent that. I'd heard her say those words with my very
own ears! Mom finally did serve dinner that night, but it was just
cold sandwiches. And she definitely seemed worried
about something. As we sat at the table eating, she stared off
into space. "Mom, what are you thinking about?" I
asked suddenly. "What?" she
said, startled. I repeated
my question. "What are you
thinking about?" "I was just thinking about all the bills I have to pay,"
said Mom. My stomach did a
little flip. "So you're really worried
about money?" "Iggy, stop being weird,"
said Tate. My mother patted
my hand. "You should be thinking about homework, Iggy, not bills," she
said. Then she quickly started talking about something
else. I got up early the next day to walk to school with
Josh. He likes to get there early, and this morning I needed to talk to
him. I got downstairs just as Josh was headed out the
door. "Can I walk to school with you?" I
asked. "I have something I want to tell
you." "Sure," said
Josh. "I'm worried about my
mom," I blurted out as we started
walking. "Why?" asked
Josh. "I think she needs money," I
said. "She's worried about paying
bills." "My dad worries about bills too," said
Josh. We walked past the Green Apple
Supermarket. That's where Josh and Jenny's dad
works. He brings home lots of food for dinner, like steak and apple
pie. So Josh didn't have to worry about having good dinners
either! "My dad even works on the weekends, to make extra money for our family," Josh went
on. "He performs magic
shows. He's working on a new trick using a one-way
mirror." "What's a one-way mirror?" I
asked. "It's a mirror on one side," explained
Josh. "But on the other side, you can see through it, like
glass." "Oh," I said,
nodding. I was pretty sure I'd seen mirrors like that on TV police
shows. "Maybe I could invent a money-making machine," I said, thinking out
loud. "I could print thousands of dollar bills, and then we'd be
rich!" Josh stopped and looked at
me. "Iggy, that's the worst idea in the
world!" "Boy," I
thought. "Josh either really likes an idea, or he really doesn't like
it!" "What's wrong with a money-printing machine?" I asked
him. "Printing money is a crime," said
Josh. "If you invent a money-printing machine, you could go to jail!"
"Jail?" I echoed.
"Oh well. Forget that invention then."
A second later Josh and I passed the candy store near school.
My mouth watered as I looked at all the delicious candy.
"I really wish I were rich now," I murmured.
"Then I could buy this whole candy store!"
I dug into my pocket and found some change.
Josh had some too.
Together, we had enough to buy a chocolate candy bar.
We decided to save it for lunchtime.
"If only I knew what my mom was thinking," I said as we walked on.
"Then I would know what to do."
Josh shook his head.
"Grown-ups are pretty mysterious.
You'd need a really great invention to figure them out!"
That's when I got my greatest idea ever.
"What if I could invent a magic thinking box?
Then I'd be able to read people's thoughts!"
At school I opened my backpack to show Molly the bell for Caswell.
But the bell was gone!
Before I could tell Molly about it, Mrs. Romano made a surprise announcement.
"Class, I have something exciting to share!"
"Are we going to have an ice cream party?" asked Colby.
"Or take a trip to the zoo?" said Ruby.
"Maybe we're getting a class pet.
I'd like a monkey!" said Kristin.
Mrs. Romano smiled.
"No, we're not getting a monkey.
There's going to be an Invention Convention in our own city!" she said.
I sat up straighter in my chair.
"An Invention Convention will be held one week from today," Mrs. Romano said.
"Students can exhibit their inventions, and there will be prizes for the best ones."
"An Invention Convention?"
I thought, forgetting about my bell problem. "Wow!"
Molly raised her hand.
"What do you get for first prize, Mrs. Romano?"
"First prize is a blue ribbon and one hundred dollars!" our teacher told us.
I let out a low whistle.
One hundred dollars!
I wondered if that was enough to help my mom.
Then I started thinking about the magic thinking box again.
That was an even better invention than Caswell's bell.
If I could make a box that worked, I might win a prize.
And then I could figure out what my mom was so worried about!
That afternoon Josh, Jenny, Molly, and I walked home from school together.
"Did your teacher tell you about the Invention Convention?" I asked Josh.
"Yes," said Josh.
"I'd like to invent an automatic homework machine."
"We'd never have to do homework again!" said Jenny.
Molly was chewing bubble gum.
"I'd like to invent gum that doesn't lose its flavor,"
she said, popping a big bubble.
"Iggy, you could build your magic thinking box for the convention!" said Josh.
"You just read my mind!" I told him.
"What's a magic thinking box?" asked Molly.
"It's a special box," I explained.
"You put it on your head, and then I can tell what you're thinking."
Molly looked puzzled.
"But how does it work?" she wanted to know.
I was glad we had reached our apartment building by then.
Because I didn't have an answer for Molly's question.
The truth is, I had no idea how my magic thinking box would work.
I just hoped it would work.
Upstairs, my mom was on the phone again.
"Well, I just don't have enough money," she said.
I couldn't believe it.
She was talking about money again too!
I went into my room and threw my backpack on the floor.
Tate was doing his homework.
"Move that backpack!" he yelled.
"It's on my side of the room again!"
"Just barely!" I argued back.
"Boys, please!" my mother called.
"I'm on the telephone."
I kicked my backpack under my bed.
At least Tate couldn't say that was on his side of the room.
Then I flopped onto my bed.
I needed to think about my magic thinking box.
How would it work, anyway?
I wanted to win a prize at the Invention Convention more than anything.
I also wanted to find out what was bothering my mom.
But how was I going to make a magic thinking box?
I'd need real magic for that.
I remembered Mr. Chen's one-way mirror.
You could see through it on one side, Josh had said.
But on the other side, it was just like a regular mirror.
Maybe a one-way mirror was exactly what I needed for my new invention!
I rushed downstairs and knocked on the door to Josh's apartment.
"Hi," I blurted out when Josh came to the door.
"Can I see your dad's one-way mirror?"
Mr. Chen appeared behind Josh with a smile.
"Follow me," he said.
Josh, Jenny, and I followed Mr. Chen into a small room off the hall.
It was the first time I had ever been inside Mr. Chen's magic room.
It was amazing!
The room was filled with all sorts of magic props and supplies.
There were top hats, colored boxes, packs of cards, and gold coins.
There were balls of different sizes, colorful feathers, even a large saw.
Mr. Chen led me over to something that looked like a small window.
Josh had told me what a one-way mirror was, but I still had questions.
"I don't understand exactly how it works," I told Mr. Chen.
"Well," he replied, "imagine one person in a bright room and another person in a dark room.
The mirror is between them."
"Okay," I said, picturing that in my mind. "Now what?"
"When the person in the bright room looks at the mirror, all he sees is himself," Mr. Chen went on.
"Got it," I said.
Mr. Chen grinned.
"But when the person in the dark room looks at the mirror, he sees something different.
He sees the other person through the glass!"
"Wow," I said. By now I was thinking hard.
I was thinking so hard, my brain hurt.
"I think I know how to make a magic thinking box," I said finally.
"How?" asked Jenny.
"Can I borrow your one-way mirror, Mr. Chen?" I asked.
"Sure," said Mr. Chen. "I actually have an extra one."
He picked up a smaller one-way mirror and handed it to me.
"Now I just need scissors, a flashlight, and a cardboard box," I said.
I ran upstairs and got some scissors.
I also got Molly so she could join in the fun.
Jenny found a flashlight, and Josh got an old box from the Green Apple Supermarket.
First I cut a hole out of the cardboard box with the scissors.
It was just a tiny bit smaller than the one-way mirror.
Next I fitted the mirror into the hole.
"Now," I said, "who wants to try the magic thinking box first?"
"Me!" cried Molly. "Let me try it!"
"Okay," I said. "Put the box over your head."
Molly put the box over her head.
"It's dark in here," she said in a muffled voice.
"I can't see anything at all."
"Just a minute!"
I handed her the flashlight.
"Now turn this on and shine it into the box," I told her.
Molly turned on the flashlight inside the box.
Then I turned off the light in the room.
"Can you see us?" I asked Molly.
"No," said Molly.
"All I can see is myself in the mirror."
"We can see you though!" cried Josh.
"It works!" I shouted.
"No, it doesn't," said Molly.
"You can see me, but you can't tell what I'm thinking!"
I looked at her face through the glass.
Her eyes were bright, and she was grinning.
"She looks excited," I thought.
But she also looked a little suspicious of my box.
"You're thinking that you want me to put on the box," I said.
"So that you can tell what I'm thinking."
Molly gasped. "That's right, Iggy!"
She yanked the box off her head and looked at me.
"Iggy," she said. "You did it!
You invented a magic thinking box!"
"Way to go!" said Josh, giving me a high five.
I grinned. My magic thinking box actually worked!
Mr. Chen said I could use his mirror for a while longer.
So I carried the magic box upstairs to my apartment.
Molly came with me.
I knew what I wanted to do next with it.
I wanted to try to read my mother's thoughts.
All I had to do was persuade Mom to put her head inside the box.
Tate was in the living room.
"What's that?" he asked, looking at my box.
"A magic thinking box," I said.
"I'm bringing it to the Invention Convention."
"It looks weird," said Tate.
"What's it supposed to do?"
"When you put it over your head, Iggy can tell what you're thinking!" said Molly.
"Want to try it?" I asked.
"Okay," said Tate.
"But you'll never be able to tell what I'm thinking."
Tate put the box over his head, and I gave him the flashlight.
"Now turn on the flashlight," I said.
Tate turned the flashlight on inside the magic thinking box.
I turned off the light in the room.
"I can see you," I said.
"But you can't see me."
"Big deal," said Tate.
"You still can't tell what I'm thinking."
"Yes, I can," I said.
"You're thinking this is a dumb invention."
Tate took the box off his head with a big grin.
"Well, you got that right!" he said.
"See, Iggy's invention works!" said Molly.
"Let's try it on my mom now," I whispered to Molly.
Molly and I went into the kitchen.
For once Mom wasn't on the phone.
She was baking cookies, just like a normal mother.
"Will you try my new invention, Mom?" I asked.
I showed her the box.
"It really works, Mrs. Erickson!" added Molly.
My mom slid a tray of cookies into the oven and then looked at me.
"What do I have to do?"
"Just put the box over your head," I said.
"You want me to put my head in that box?" said Mom.
"Just for a minute, Mom," I said. "Please?"
"Well, okay." Mom sat down, and I put the box over her head.
Molly laughed. "You look funny, Mrs. Erickson!"
"I feel funny," said Mom.
"It's very dark in here."
"Here's the flashlight," I said.
"Molly, can you please turn off the kitchen light?"
Pretty soon Molly and I were looking through the one-way mirror.
"All I can see is myself," said Mom.
"We can see you," I told her.
I stared at Mom's face.
She was frowning as she stared at herself in the glass.
"And I can tell what you're thinking!"
"Really?" said Mom. "What?"
"You're thinking about money!" I said.
"About how you're going to get some!"
Mom took off the box.
"Your invention works, Iggy.
I was thinking about money—about how I need a whole bank!"
Molly and I looked at each other.
I didn't need a magic box to read her mind this time.
I already knew what Molly was thinking because it was exactly what I was thinking.
What if I hadn't invented the story about Mom planning to rob a bank?
What if it was true?
Soon the cookies were done, and the kitchen was full of delicious smells.
Josh and Jenny came up to my apartment, and we all ate the chewy chocolate cookies.
I decided to enjoy the cookies and stop worrying about Mom for a little while.
"Robbing a bank takes lots of planning," I told myself.
If Mom was going to rob her bank, she couldn't do it right away.
Plus, I needed my brain for something else besides worrying:
getting ready for the Invention Convention.
I was in bed that night when I remembered the bell for Caswell.
I'd first thought of it so he wouldn't get lost.
But now the bell was lost!
I turned on my light.
"Hey, turn that off!" yelled Tate.
"I lost something," I mumbled.
I looked and looked, but there was no sign of the bell.
Finally I gave up and went back to bed.
I hoped I could find it before Caswell got lost again.
At school everyone was excited about the Invention Convention.
Molly had invented a way to keep crayons from breaking.
She put each crayon into a straw.
Unlike my coloring machine, her idea really worked!
But the big hit was my magic thinking box.
Everyone wanted to put it on.
"Let me go first, Iggy!" said Kristin.
"Then it's my turn!" said Colby.
"Wait a minute!" I said.
"The Invention Convention is next week.
I don't want to use up all the magic before then!"
Everyone agreed this was a good idea.
I thought it was a good idea too.
Because the truth was, I wasn't positive my invention actually worked.
I thought it did.
I hoped it did.
But maybe I had just made some lucky guesses.
The next week seemed to drag by, but at last the big day arrived.
All the kids with inventions boarded the bus to go to the Convention Center.
Josh had invented an alarm.
It went off when Bunch tried to eat Sparky's hamster food.
Jenny had invented a bath for Sparky.
Molly brought her crayon invention.
And I held my magic thinking box carefully on my lap.
The convention was in a big building downtown.
We set up our inventions on tables, and the judges walked around, examining them.
One judge admired Molly's crayon invention.
"Your crayons will never break!" said Molly.
"Very clever!" he said.
A girl from another school had invented special glasses.
They had a picture of wide-open eyes pasted on them.
"You can put them on and go to sleep in math class," she explained.
"The teacher will think you are awake!"
Next the judges stopped at Josh's table.
He showed them how his dog buzzer alarm worked.
It made such a loud noise that one judge jumped!
Jenny's table was next to mine.
She showed the judges a bowl filled with soapy water.
Then she put Sparky and his hamster wheel inside the bowl.
When Sparky spun around on his wheel, he got clean in the water.
"It gets all the dust off him," said Jenny.
"So he doesn't make me sneeze!"
"Ah-choo!" One of the judges sneezed.
"Hamsters always make me sneeze!" she said.
Finally the judges came to my table.
"What an interesting box," one judge remarked.
I told them how it worked.
"Amazing!" said the judge who had sneezed.
"Can I try it?"
"Sure." I proudly handed her my box.
"Put the box over your head," I said.
Next I handed her the flashlight.
"Now turn the flashlight on."
She followed my instructions.
"I can see myself," I heard her say.
In the dim room, I could easily see the judge through the one-way mirror.
But even though I'd made some lucky guesses before, my luck was running out now.
Inside the box the judge wasn't smiling, but she wasn't frowning either.
As I looked at her, I had no idea what she was thinking.
I was about to make a wild guess.
Then suddenly I noticed Sparky spinning fast on his wheel.
He flew out of the bowl and hit the floor.
Then he raced toward the judge who was wearing my box!
Sparky raced past the judges.
"Sparky, come back!" yelled Jenny.
Josh tried to grab Sparky.
But the hamster was so slippery from soap and water, he slipped through Josh's fingers.
Then Sparky ran toward a judge—the one who was wearing my magic thinking box!
The judge sneezed loudly. "Ah-choo!"
She sneezed so hard that the box flew off her head.
It landed right on top of Sparky!
Sparky was scared.
He didn't like being trapped in a dark box.
So he ran faster than ever.
"Ha-ha! Look at that box!"
One of the kids laughed.
"It has legs!"
The boy was right.
Sparky's legs stuck out as the box moved across the floor.
It looked like the box was running all by itself!
Soon all the kids were laughing as Sparky raced around the big room.
Even the judges laughed.
The judge who had tried out my magic thinking box laughed the hardest of all.
Sparky raced under a table and knocked it over.
Finally Josh caught up with him, and he lifted the magic thinking box off his hamster.
"Sparky!" he said. "I'm so glad I caught you!"
I ran up to Josh, and a group of kids followed me.
"I bet I know what Sparky was thinking," I said.
"What?" a bunch of kids asked.
"Sparky was probably thinking, 'Help! Get me out of this box!'"
Some kids laughed, but I sighed.
I might be right about Sparky's thoughts, but I wasn't going to win a prize.
I hadn't even had a chance to show the judges how my invention worked.
Soon it was time for the judges to choose the winners.
One judge announced third prize.
A boy who had invented a bicycle fan to keep him cool on hot days won that.
Next the judge announced second prize.
"This prize goes to Susie Johnson for inventing a new use for old CDs—wearing them as earrings!"
All the kids clapped as Susie went up to claim the red ribbon.
Everyone waited for the judge to announce first prize.
"First prize and one hundred dollars goes to Jenny Chen for her hamster bath!"
The kids shouted and whistled as Jenny accepted the money.
The judge put a big blue ribbon on Sparky's cage.
I was happy for Jenny.
She deserved to win.
But I was sad for me.
It was clear that I wasn't a very good inventor.
I hadn't even won third prize.
