I'm normally a calm person.
But at that moment I blew up.
Everything was going wrong!
My Amazing Mess-Pusher had caused our plot list to get thrown out.
Molly was still not sleeping.
And Tate was being mean and driving me crazy!
"I can't stand it!" I yelled. "Nothing is going right!"
Then I kicked the garbage bag as hard as I could.
When I kicked the garbage bag, stuff fell all over the floor.
Now, on top of everything else going wrong in my life, I had a mess to clean up!
I started picking things up.
The papers were slimy because there was also a banana peel inside.
I guess I had left that in my old room too.
No wonder Tate had wanted me out of there!
A magazine from the bag had slid under my bed.
I reached under and grabbed it.
It was one of my nature magazines.
The cover showed some monkeys in a tree.
At first I didn't know why all these things—schoolwork, monkeys, bananas—reminded me of Matilda Mackey's book The Wicky Wacky School .
Then suddenly I knew the reason.
They were all part of her book's plot!
At that moment I, Iggy, had my most brilliant idea ever.
I would create a plot inventor!
The next day I sat down at my desk and started cutting little pieces of paper.
Then I wrote a different word on each piece of paper.
I did this until I couldn't think of any more good words.
I could smell coffee coming from the kitchen where my mom was making breakfast.
Tate was sitting at the table, eating leftover spaghetti.
He likes cold spaghetti for breakfast.
Have I mentioned that my brother is really weird?
"Mom, do you have any old magazines?" I asked.
"Old magazines?" asked my mom.
"What do you need them for?"
"Probably for another one of his crazy ideas," said Tate.
"My idea is not crazy," I said.
"I am working on an incredible invention."
Tate rolled his eyes.
He always thought my ideas were crazy.
But I wasn't going to let that bother me now.
I knew I had a good idea, and I needed to stay focused.
"There are a few magazines in the living room," said my mom.
"You can have them, Iggy."
I got the magazines and went back to my room.
I picked up my scissors and began cutting out all the pictures.
Soon I had a big pile.
I gathered all the pieces of paper and all the pictures.
I put them in a big box and cut some holes in the lid.
I realized I hadn't eaten breakfast yet.
So on my way out the door, I grabbed the last chocolate granola bar.
I could hear Tate complaining about that as I walked down the hallway.
When I got to school, Mrs. Romano asked me what was in the box.
I told her all about my plot inventor.
She looked at all the small pieces of paper in the box, and I explained how it worked.
"Wow, Iggy," said Mrs. Romano. "That's a very clever idea!"
"Can we try it out?" I asked.
"Certainly," said Mrs. Romano.
She made an announcement to the class after circle time.
"We are going to work on our stories now," she said.
"I know some of you are having trouble thinking of exciting plots."
"I still don't understand how to write a middle," said Gina.
"I don't know how to make something go wrong," added Colby.
Mrs. Romano beamed. "Iggy has invented something that could help all of you.
Iggy, would you like to show everyone how it works?"
Suddenly I felt my stomach flip-flop.
Either my plot inventor was a brilliant idea, or it was a really, really dumb one.
Carrying my plot inventor, I walked to the front of the classroom.
"It looks like a box," said Jake.
"It is a box," I said.
"But because of what's in it, it's also something really cool—a plot inventor."
"Oh boy . . . ," someone muttered.
"It's another one of Iggy's incredible inventions."
"What's in the box?"
Gina wanted to know.
"Something that will make writing a story really easy," I explained.
"Lots of words and pictures.
All you have to do is shake the box."
Everyone watched while I gave the box a good shake.
"Then you turn it over and let a few pieces of paper fall onto the floor."
Three words and one picture fluttered through the holes in the lid.
I picked them up and showed them to the class.
"This is a picture of shoes," I said.
"And there's a word on each of these pieces of paper . . . 'sleep,' 'house,' and 'cake.'" Everyone
just stared at me. "Now
what do you do?" asked Colby. "Well,"
I said, not entirely sure. "Now you—" "Ooh!"
cried Gina. "That gave me a great idea, Iggy! My
story is about a fox and a hunter. The
fox wants to stop the hunter from hunting in the woods. Now
I know what the fox can do—wait until the hunter is sleeping .
Then the fox can sneak into the hunter's house and steal his shoes.
Without shoes, the hunter can't go hunting.
At the end of the story, Fox and the other animals will celebrate with . . . cake
!" Everyone was
amazed. I could hardly believe it
either. My plot inventor
worked! All the kids lined up to take turns using the plot
inventor. Pretty soon everyone was writing, and no one was stuck
anymore. Mrs. Romano said the plot machine was one of the best inventions she'd ever
seen. "Iggy, may I let the other fourth-grade class use it for their stories?" she
asked. Proudly, I told Mrs. Romano that was just
fine. Earlier I said that no one was stuck on their stories anymore, but that wasn't quite
true. There were two people who were still stuck: Molly and
me! After shaking the box, we had decided to write about the giant talking
vacuum. So we decided the vacuum wouldn't suck up the whole
world. Instead the boy in the story, Jack, would use the vacuum to clean his
room. The vacuum sucked up his bed, his clothes, and even his
computer. But that wasn't
all. The giant vacuum sucked up his older
brother! Hmm . . . I wonder where I got that idea!
Our story was really funny.
But we couldn't figure out the last part—how to get Jack's brother out of the vacuum.
And we had to finish our stories by Friday.
At recess Molly and I bounced ideas off some other kids.
"Jack could just leave his brother inside the vacuum," suggested Jake.
I liked Jake's idea, but Molly got upset.
"Jack wouldn't do that!" she said.
"He really wants his brother back."
"He could smash the vacuum and get his brother out," suggested Evan.
But Molly and I both liked the giant talking vacuum, so we didn't want anyone to break it.
When I got home, Tate yelled at me for taking the last chocolate granola bar this morning.
By now I was ready to suck him up with a giant vacuum cleaner!

episodes.title: A Good Night for a Fire

subtitle.text: There's one really cool thing about our apartment.
Well, actually, there are two really cool things.
The first cool thing is my bedroom, where I do most of my inventing.
The second cool thing is our fireplace.
Most apartment buildings don't have fireplaces.
But our building is really old, and there are lots of fireplaces.
We have one in our living room.
Shortly after Tate stopped yelling at me for taking the last granola bar, my mom came home from work.
It was raining outside.
Thunder boomed and lightning flashed.
"This is a good night to make a fire," my mom said.
So after dinner my mom built a fire in the fireplace.
Molly, Josh, and Jenny came over.
We all sat on the rug in front of the crackling fire.
We played cards while the rain beat against the windows.
Soon Molly fell asleep.
She still wasn't getting much sleep because of bad dreams about monsters.
We let Molly sleep and played cards without her.
I was getting sleepy myself when I heard the wail of a fire engine.
Then came the sound of a smoke detector in our building.
Molly woke up suddenly.
"Is the apartment on fire?" she cried.
"No," my mom said. "Everything is fine here."
I glanced at the fire in our fireplace.
The fire was almost out.
But the sound of the siren was really close now.
I ran to our front windows and looked out.
"The fire truck stopped in front of our building!" I cried.
"And the firefighters are jumping out!"
My mom looked alarmed.
"Uh-oh. We'd better get out of the building fast!" she said.
Most of the people who lived in our building were already standing outside on the sidewalk. Mr.
Chen was there, and Molly's mom and dad were there with Caswell. They
rushed over and gave Molly a hug. "I
called the fire department," said Molly's dad. "Our
TV exploded!" Most
little kids would be scared. But
not Caswell! Instead
he was grinning and looking pretty excited. "There
was a big bang and lots of smoke!" We
watched the firefighters enter the buidling. They
were wearing special helmets and carrying long hoses. Soon
they came outside again. One
was carrying Molly's TV. "Everything
is fine," the firefighter told Molly's parents. "Except
for your TV," added another firefighter. "I
guess you'll need to buy a new one." "Maybe
one of the monsters from Monster Madness made it explode," said Caswell. The
first firefighter laughed. "I
don't think that was the reason," he said. "The
fire was probably caused by the lightning." "Thank
goodness we're all safe!" said Mrs. O'Donnell. I
noticed that Molly didn't look sleepy anymore. She
looked happy. Just
before we all went back inside, she leaned over to me. "Iggy,"
she whispered. "This
is the best thing that ever happened!" "The
fire truck coming to our building?" I said in surprise. "No,"
said Molly. "My family's TV exploding." She
grinned. "No more watching Monster Madness after school every day!" I
nodded. I hadn't invented anything to solve Molly's problem, but it had solved itself. Molly
didn't have to worry about scary monster shows anymore. Molly's
parents left the TV sitting out on the curb. "Good-bye,
TV!" said Molly happily. There
was one thing she didn't expect though. Her
mom and dad bought another TV the next day! So
Caswell and Lucy went back to watching Monster Madness .
And poor Molly went back to not sleeping.
I still couldn't think of an invention to help Molly.
I did suddenly get an idea for the ending of our story though.
It happened when I was pouring myself some Crunchy Oats cereal on Wednesday morning.
I shook the last few crumbs into my bowl.
I tried to get a new box from the cupboard, but I couldn't reach it.
Even when I stood on a stool, the box was just out of reach.
"Mom, I can't reach the cereal!" I called.
My mom was in the living room, putting on her coat.
"I'm late for work, Iggy," she said.
"Please ask your brother to help."
"He won't do it!" I said. "He never helps me."
I don't think my mom heard me, because she said good-bye and hurried out the door.
"You took the last chocolate granola bar," said Tate, staring at me.
"And now you're eating all the Crunchy Oats!"
"There's a brand-new box," I started to say.
"But I can't . . ."
To my surprise, Tate smiled at me.
"I'm just kidding," he said.
"I'll get the cereal for you."
Tate reached up and grabbed the box of Crunchy Oats cereal.
"Gee, thanks!" I said.
"All you have to do is ask," said Tate.
"What?" I blinked in surprise.
All you have to do is ask?
That was it!
The boy in our story could ask the giant vacuum to give his brother back.
The giant vacuum was friendly and gentle.
The vacuum would be happy to return Jack's stuff, along with his big brother.
And Jack would be happy to have his big brother around again.
Just like me.
Once in a while anyway.
Molly loved my plan for our story ending.
We titled our last chapter "Just Ask."
As we wrote the final words, I got the best idea ever—the one I'd been hoping to get. "Why
don't you tell Lucy you can't sleep because of the monster show?" I said to Molly. "Then
just ask her if she and Caswell can watch something different." "Just
ask?" echoed Molly. She
shook her head. "But
that would be admitting I'm a big baby." "No,"
I said, "it would be telling Lucy that you don't like monster shows." Molly
looked thoughtful. "Just
ask?" she repeated one more time. I
nodded. "Yep. Just ask." And
that is exactly what Molly did. She
didn't feel like a baby either because Lucy just shrugged and said, "Sure." And
Caswell said, "I'm sick of Monster Madness anyway." After
that Molly started sleeping better. And
Lucy started thinking up stuff for all of us to do after school. We
played games and read books. We
went to the playground and even made a homemade pizza together! A
few weeks later our own books were printed and placed in the school library. Molly
and I were there one day when a second-grade class came in. The
kids started looking for good books to read. I
saw a little girl pick up Jack and the Giant Vacuum .
It was the book that Molly and I had written!
"This book looks really good!" the little girl said to her friend.
And then she sat down and read the whole story!
"Wow," I thought, watching her.
A lot of my inventions, like the Enchanting Cherries bubble bath, turned into big disasters.
But this time, with Molly's help, I had invented something pretty cool—a real page-turner!
I was lying on my bed one morning, thinking about how perfect everything was.
Usually there is at least one thing wrong in my life.
Most days it has something to do with my brother, Tate.
Yesterday, for example, he got mad when I squeezed all the toothpaste out of the tube.
I was experimenting to see if I could invent an automatic toothpaste squeezer.
Or sometimes it's our dinner menu.
I hate when Mom makes eggplant casserole, which is the most disgusting food ever invented.
Whoever invented it should go to jail!
But tonight we were having pizza.
My favorite. Plus, winter vacation was coming up soon.
So I was going to have a whole week to think up a new invention.
If the invention was really good, I might even get into the Inventor's Hall of Fame!
You'd better watch out when you think everything is perfect.
Do you know why?
Because that means something big is about to go wrong!
"Iggy, the muffins are ready!" my mom called, knocking on my door.
"And I have a surprise."
Oh boy, warm muffins and a surprise!
"What's the surprise?" I asked, coming out of my room.
My brother Tate walked into the kitchen.
"Is the surprise for me too?" he asked.
"Sit down," Mom said. "And I'll tell you both."
Tate and I each took a warm muffin and sat down at the table.
"Well," she began, "last night I got a call from Aunt Julia and Uncle John."
"That's great!" I said.
"Are we going to visit them over winter vacation?"
My aunt Julia and uncle John are super-rich.
They live in a big house with a swimming pool.
Of course, it's too cold to swim in the pool in the winter.
"But maybe we can go sledding on the hill behind their house," I thought.
"And I can work on my new invention in their huge attic!"
Tate looked excited too.
"Cool," he said.
"I can stay in the bedroom with the TV like I did last year."
"I hope I don't have to share a room with Oliver again," I said.
My little cousin is a big pain.
He never shares his stuff, and he is always complaining about something.
"Well . . . ," my mother said, "actually you will be sharing a room with Oliver, Iggy."
"Too bad!" Tate said, grinning at me.
I shrugged. "That's okay," I said.
"I guess I can stand being stuck in Oliver's room for a few days."
"You don't understand," my mom said, "we're not going to your aunt and uncle's house."
"What do you mean?" I asked.
"Are we all going on a trip together?"
"No," my mom said. "Oliver is coming to visit us.
He'll be sharing your bedroom, Iggy."
"What?" I practically shouted.
"Calm down, Iggy," said Mom.
"It's only for a short time."
"But why does he have to come here?" I asked.
"And why does he have to share my room?
Why can't he share with Tate?"
"No way!" said Tate.
"He can't share with me.
I'm a teenager."
"Well, I'm an inventor," I said.
"And I'm on the brink of a major invention.
It's going to win me a place in the Inventor's Hall of Fame!"
You need quiet time to think up a great invention.
I could forget about quiet time with Oliver around.
"It will be fine, Iggy," my mom said. "You'll see."
I saw something, all right.
I saw that my winter vacation was going to be horrible.
What did I tell you?
When things seem perfect, something big always goes wrong!
As soon as I finished my muffin, I went across the hall to Molly's apartment.
Molly came to the door wearing her purple bathrobe and eating a chocolate-covered donut.
"I'm having a mental health day," Molly announced.
Tate had told me all about mental health days.
You get to sit around in your pajamas, watching TV and eating your favorite foods.
"Well, I'm having an emergency!" I said.
Molly stopped chewing her donut.
"What's wrong?" she asked. "Is somebody sick?"
I shook my head.
"No one is sick—except me.
I'm sick of my cousin, Oliver, and he isn't even here yet!" Molly
looked puzzled. "Iggy,"
she said. "What
are you talking about?" "I'm
talking about my bratty cousin, Oliver," I said. "He's
coming to visit, and he's going to share my room!" I
told Molly about Oliver visiting over winter vacation. "My
mom said Aunt Julia and Uncle John want to take a cruise," I added. "Without
Oliver?" asked Molly. I
nodded. "My uncle has been working really hard. They
want to take a vacation by themselves." Molly
giggled. "They probably want to get away from Oliver for a while!" "I
bet you're right," I said glumly. "But
why do they have to leave him with us?" Just
then we heard Josh and Jenny walking up the stairs with their dad. Molly
and I looked down. They
were all carrying grocery bags. "I've
got a problem!" I burst out. Josh
looked up at me. "Really?"
he said. "Maybe
we'd better have a powwow." My
friends and I have a "powwow" whenever somebody has a big problem. We
get together to figure out a solution. "That's
a great idea!" I said. "I'll
go get dressed," said Molly. "A
powwow sounds like more fun than a mental health day." "We'll meet
in five minutes outside on the front steps!" said Josh. Soon we
were all sitting on the front steps. But it
was freezing outside, and an icy rain had started to fall. "Let's go
inside by the radiator," said Jenny. We went
into the front hall and stood by the big radiator. It was
making loud banging noises. But at
least the front hall was warm. I told
Josh and Jenny about Oliver's coming to visit. "And he's
going to share my room!" I groaned. "So I
won't have any quiet time to work on a new invention. And I
really wanted to get into the Inventor's Hall of Fame!" "How do
you do that?" asked Josh. "You have
to invent something really amazing," I explained. "And if
you do invent something cool, you win a trophy. Plus, you
get your picture on the Inventor's Hall of Fame website." Molly's face
lit up. "You would
be famous, Iggy!" "But now
Oliver is coming," I said. "He'll spoil
everything!" "It could
be fun," said Josh. He was
trying to cheer me up. "You'll be
like a big brother to Oliver." " Me
, a big brother?" I said. I
had to admit I hadn't thought of that. "We
could fix him a cute little bed in your room," Jenny chimed in. "And
invent games and fun activities to do!" added Molly. I
smiled. "You guys are the best friends ever!" I said. I
was starting to feel a little better. Maybe
Oliver's visit wouldn't be so bad after all. I'm
glad I didn't have a crystal ball to see the future right then. Because
if I'd had a crystal ball, I would have seen the truth. Oliver
was going to be trouble— big trouble!
I may not live in a mansion.
And we don't have a swimming pool.
But I have the best friends in the world, who live right in my apartment building!
We can visit each other without even going outside.
I was glad for that on Saturday.
Because the icy rain kept falling all day.
After our powwow the four of us made a bed in my room for Oliver.
Caswell helped too.
We started with a thick pad that Josh had taken to Boy Scouts camp last summer.
We spread out my sleeping bag on top of that.
Then Molly added a pillow in the shape of a frog.
Mom looked in to see what we were doing.
"What a cute bed!" she said.
"I'm sure Oliver will love it."
She ruffled my hair.
"I'm glad to see you have a good attitude, Iggy."
My friends stayed for dinner that night.
While we ate pizza, we planned all the fun we would have with Oliver.
"We can have a cookout in front of our fireplace," I said.
"And roast marshmallows," said Caswell.
"We can play Princesses and Pirates on the computer," said Jenny.
"I'll let Oliver play with my marble run too," I said.
"I'll be just like a big brother.
Well, a nice big brother,"
I added, shooting a look at Tate.
Tate rolled his eyes.
"You think it's easy to be a big brother?"
I made a face at him.
"It's easier than being a little brother," I said.
"Just wait," said Tate. "You'll see."
"Well, at least I have a good attitude about Oliver," I said.
"Don't I, Mom?"
My mom laughed.
"You do have a good attitude about Oliver," she said.
"But you might want to adjust your attitude toward your brother."
When grown-ups say you "might want" to do something, they mean you should do it.
"How's my attitude?"
asked Caswell, his face smeared with tomato sauce.
"Your attitude is fine," said Molly, "but your face is a mess."
Oliver was arriving with Aunt Julia and Uncle John the next day.
By now I was actually looking forward to it!
The next morning was bright and cold.
Jenny, Josh, Molly and Caswell came over to wait for Oliver.
We all stood looking out the front window to the street.
"What color is their car?" asked Josh.
"I don't know," I said.
"They buy a new one every year."
A long black limousine cruised down the street.
"That must be them!" cried Molly.
"Wow, they really are rich!"
But the black limousine rolled right by.
Next we saw an ambulance race down the street.
"Maybe that's them," said Jenny, "and they're having an emergency."
But the ambulance whizzed past our building.
After that a moving van rumbled down the street.
"Maybe that's them," I said, "and they're moving in for good!"
"Ha-ha!" Tate smirked as he came into the living room.
"You'll have to share your bedroom forever, Iggy!"
"Why would they want to live with us?" I said.
"They have a big house of their own."
"Maybe they lost all their money in the stock market," said Tate.
"Huh?" said Jenny, looking confused.
"Don't pay any attention to Tate," I said.
"He thinks he's so smart just because he's in high school."
At that moment a knock came at the door.
We ran to see who it was.
There stood Aunt Julia and Uncle John.
And beside them was Oliver.
Their car had pulled up without our even seeing it!
"Hello!" cried Aunt Julia with a big smile.
"Hi!" said Uncle John.
"I am not staying here even for one minute!" shouted Oliver.
Aunt Julia and Uncle John ignored Oliver's screaming.
I can tell you that it wasn't easy because he was screaming really loud
. They just acted like everything was
normal. "Well," said Aunt Julia, "our cruise ship leaves in two
hours." "That's right. We don't want to miss the boat!" said Uncle
John. "So long,
Oliver. You have our cell phone
numbers!" "I'm not staying here!" yelled
Oliver. "We'll be back before you know
it," said Aunt Julia, giving Oliver a
hug. "Don't forget to brush your teeth,
sweetie." And then they were
gone. "Hey, Oliver," I said, before he could start screaming
again. "Want to see the bed we made for you on the
floor? It's right next to
mine." Oliver shook his
head. "I want to go home!" he
cried. Mom put her arm around
him. "I'm sure you'll be very happy here, Oliver," she said.
"We'll have lots of fun."
Oliver opened his mouth to start yelling again. "I want—"
"Let's play Princesses and Pirates !" interrupted
Jenny. Oliver shut his
mouth. "That's a stupid game," he said in a grumpy
voice. Boy, if anyone needed an attitude adjustment, it was
Oliver. "Would you like a hot dog, Oliver?" asked my
mom. Oliver shook his
head. "My mom says hot dogs are bad for you," he
said. "She says you don't know what's really in
them." "What's really in them?" I
asked. "Slimy snake guts," said
Oliver. Josh and I burst out
laughing. Oliver seemed surprised that we thought that was
funny. Oliver complained all through
dinner. At bedtime I took him to my
room. I showed him the bed we'd made on the
floor. "And look, my room has a skylight," I
said. "You can see the
moon." I pointed to the
skylight. But Oliver did not seem interested in the
moon. Instead he took his toothbrush out of his
suitcase. "You have to brush your teeth in the kitchen," I
explained. "Why?" asked
Oliver. "Because there's no sink in our bathroom," I
said. "Who ever heard of that?" said
Oliver. Our bathroom is kind of
weird. First of all, it's right next to the
kitchen. And because it's so small, there's no room for a
sink. That's why you have to brush your teeth in the
kitchen. "Boy, that's the smallest bathroom I ever
saw," said Oliver when he came back to my
room. "Our bathroom at home is as big as your whole
kitchen." By now I was sick of listening to Oliver
complain. I just wanted him to go to
sleep! Oliver lay down on his bed.
I turned out the light.
"I've never slept on the floor before," he said.
He didn't sound too happy.
I closed my eyes and pretended to be asleep.
"You gave me a frog pillow," said Oliver.
"I hate frogs!"
I started snoring very loudly.
"I can't sleep with a frog pillow!" wailed Oliver.
"I hate the color green!"
He kept moaning and complaining.
I tossed and turned in my bed.
Finally I sat up.
"I give up!" I shouted.
"You can have my bed!
I'll sleep on the floor!"
To my surprise there was no answer from Oliver.
I leaned over and looked at him.
He was curled up on his bed in the moonlight, sound asleep.
"Thank goodness!" I thought.
As I lay back down, I realized something.
Tate was right.
Being a big brother was a lot harder than I had thought.
The next day Josh, Jenny, Molly, and I took Oliver to the park.
The rain had frozen overnight, and the park pathways were slippery with ice.
Molly slipped on the ice. "Ahh!"
"My feet are freezing," complained Oliver.
"Mine too," said Josh, stomping his feet.
"I wish Iggy could invent something to keep our feet warm."
"Oliver, did you know that Iggy is an inventor?" asked Jenny.
"What's an inventor?" asked Oliver.
"It's someone who invents things to solve problems," I said proudly.
Maybe Oliver would realize that his big cousin Iggy was special.
Instead Oliver just scowled.
"Big deal," he mumbled.
I scowled back at him.
Then I went back to thinking about an invention that would keep our feet warm.
My mom had a hair dryer.
"What if I made a special holder for the shoes?" I thought.
"Then I could blow the hot dryer inside the shoes!
That might work!"
We headed home about an hour later.
"My feet are soo cold!" Oliver complained.
"It was a dumb idea to go outside."
"Why don't you take your shoes off," I said.
To my surprise Oliver listened to me and took his shoes off by the fireplace.
My mom had built a fire there.
While we were drinking hot cocoa, I asked Mom if I could borrow her hair dryer.
She narrowed her eyes. "What for?"
"A shoe-warming invention," I explained.
"How will it work?" she wanted to know.
"I'm not sure," I said. "I have to experiment."
Mom shook her head.
"I don't think I want you to experiment with my hair dryer," she said.
"It's brand-new. If something goes wrong, I'll have to buy another one."
Oliver looked miserable.
"Now my socks are cold,"
he whined, swinging his feet under the kitchen table.
I was getting better at ignoring him.
"It would be great if I could keep our shoes warm while we were outside," I thought.
I imagined walking down an icy street with toasty warm feet.
That would feel fantastic.
I went back into the living room and stared at the blazing fire.
What if I used the fire to warm up shoes?
The other kids were still in the kitchen.
I could hear Josh telling jokes.
"Why did the farmer throw the clock out the window?" he asked.
"Why?" asked Molly.
"He wanted to see time fly!"
"Ha-ha!" Molly and Jenny laughed.
"I don't get it," said Oliver.
"When time goes fast, you say 'time flies,'" explained Josh.
"The farmer wanted to see time fly!
That's why he threw the clock out the window."
Somebody else started telling a joke.
I took one of Oliver's shoes and stuck it on the end of a long metal poker.
Then I propped up the poker near the fire.
Now Oliver's shoe would get nice and warm inside.
I went back to the kitchen.
Tate was telling a joke now.
"What's worse than biting into an apple and finding a big bug inside?" he asked.
"What?" asked Molly.
"Finding half a bug!" said Tate.
To my surprise Oliver actually smiled.
But Jenny made a face.
"That's disgusting!" she said.
"I would hate to eat a bug."
"Or even half a bug!" added Molly with a shudder.
Josh started telling another joke, but then suddenly he stopped.
He sniffed. "What's that smell?" he said.
"It smells like leather," Mom said. "Burning leather."
"Oh my gosh! Oliver's shoe!" I cried.
I ran into the living room.
The poker I had propped up had fallen into the fireplace.
And Oliver's shoe was on fire!
My mom grabbed the poker with Oliver's shoe and pulled it out of the fire.
The shoe was no longer in flames, but it was still smoking.
My mom hurried to the kitchen sink and ran water over the shoe.
Now Oliver's shoe was burned and wet.
Oliver started yelling.
"Iggy ruined my shoe!"
"Wow, Iggy," Tate murmured. "You really messed up."
"I was only trying to invent a shoe warmer," I said.
"Inventors are always thinking of new ideas."
"Well, you're going to have to think in your room for a while," Mom said, frowning.
"And I want you to apologize to Oliver."
"Sorry," I mumbled.
Oliver just stared down at his ruined shoe.
In my room I thought about what a bad attitude everyone had.
Well, not everyone.
But Tate had a bad attitude.
He didn't have to say I messed up.
And Oliver. He had a terrible attitude about visiting us.
I sighed. "Wouldn't it be great," I thought, "if there was something that could change people's attitudes?"
That's when I got an idea for a new invention—an Amazing Attitude Adjuster!
What a great idea!
With inventions, you have to figure out how they will actually work.
That's the hard part.
That was what had gone wrong with my shoe-warmer invention.
I hadn't thought about it enough.
But this time I was going to think a lot.
I would invent the perfect attitude adjuster!
By the time Mom said I could come out of my room, I felt happy again.
For me, an idea for a new invention is the best attitude adjuster ever.
Josh, Jenny, and Molly had gone home.
Tate was doing his homework on the computer.
Oliver was walking around the apartment with his burned shoe half on.
It had shrunk in the fire, and now it didn't fit on his foot.
"My foot hurts in this shoe!" he complained, stomping around.
"Well, why don't you take it off?" I asked.
"I can't take it off," said Oliver.
"I might get a splinter in my foot from these wood floors."
I let out a loud sigh.
Now Oliver was complaining about things that hadn't even happened yet!
Tate looked up.
"Why did the boy bury his flashlight?" he asked Oliver, winking at me.
"I don't know," said Oliver. "Why?"
"Because," said Tate, "the batteries were dead."
I started laughing.
"Ha-ha! Get it? Oliver?" I said.
"The flashlight's batteries were dead so the boy buried the flashlight!"
Oliver stopped stomping.
"That's funny!" he said, grinning.
"Tell me another joke."
Tate told Oliver another joke, and Oliver burst out laughing.
When I went into the kitchen, Mom greeted me with a smile.
"Tate's joke seemed to cheer up Oliver."
I remembered something my grandfather told me once.
He said when he was growing up, there was a service called Dial-a-Joke.
You could call a special number on the telephone.
A recording would come on and tell you a joke.
My grandfather said that calling Dial-a-Joke always put him in a great mood.
"Hmm . . . ," I thought.
I was pretty sure that Molly had an old toy telephone.
It had an old-fashioned wheel for dialing.
If I could use it to tell jokes, I could change people's attitudes.
I could make them laugh and feel happy!
"Wow, Iggy!" I told myself.
"That is a fantastic idea!"
It was more than that—it was an award-winning idea.
A "get into the Inventor's Hall of Fame" idea!
And cranky Oliver had helped me think of it!
The next morning Oliver's shoe still didn't fit.
In fact, it had shrunk even more overnight.
He complained all during breakfast.
After he finished complaining about his shoe, he complained about the pancakes.
First he complained they were too hot.
Then he complained they were too cold.
I tried to distract him with a joke.
"Guess what the patient said to his doctor?"
"I don't know," grumbled Oliver. "And I don't care!"
I ignored his bad mood.
"The patient said, 'Doctor, I get a pain in my eye whenever I drink hot cocoa.'
And the doctor said, 'Try taking the spoon out of your cup before you drink.'
Ha-ha, get it, Oliver?" I said.
"The spoon was poking him in the eye!"
Oliver looked down, so I wouldn't see him smile.
Every time he started complaining, telling a joke cheered him up.
It proved that my Amazing Attitude Adjuster was going to work!
A few minutes later Molly knocked on the door.
"The sun is out!" she said when I answered.
"Want to play on the school playground?"
That put Oliver in a bad mood again.
"I can't go out!" he cried.
"I don't have any shoes to wear!"
You would have thought he was Oliver Twist.
Oliver Twist is a poor boy in a book that my mom read to me.
He was so poor that he had to go barefoot in the street.
"Hey, Oliver, why don't we pretend you're Oliver Twist?" I suggested.
Oliver started crying harder.
"I don't want to be a different Oliver," he wailed.
"I want to be me!
And I want to go home!"
Mom was cleaning up in the kitchen.
She had taken a few days off from work for winter vacation.
"I think we need to buy Oliver some new shoes," she said.
"Molly can come with us to the shoe store."
"I can't go to the shoe store," cried Oliver.
"I don't have any shoes to wear!"
"You can borrow Iggy's old boots," said my mom.
"I think there is a pair in the closet."
Oliver complained that my old boots were too big.
He complained all the way to the shoe store.
My bad attitude about Oliver was coming back, and it was coming back stronger than ever.
I didn't complain out loud, but I complained loudly in my thoughts.
"Oliver is a big pain!
Why did he have to come visit us anyway?
I could be home now, working on my new invention.
He's ruining my chances to get into the Inventor's Hall of Fame!"
My mom bought Oliver a really cool pair of shoes.
Then we ate lunch at a cafeteria.
It's a fun place to eat because you can pick out anything you want.
Oliver chose a hamburger and four desserts!
Mom made him put back three of the desserts.
Molly and I both chose pizza and ice cream.
Oliver didn't complain while he was chewing his hamburger.
That gave me a chance to talk to Molly.
"Molly," I said, "do you still have your toy telephone?"
"Yes," said Molly.
"I saw it when we were cleaning my room with your mess-pusher."
"Can I borrow the phone for my new invention?" I asked.
"Sure," said Molly. "What is your invention?"
"It's an attitude adjuster," I said.
I looked over at Oliver and lowered my voice.
"I plan to use it on a certain person who really needs a new attitude!"
"I hope it doesn't backfire like your shoe-warmer invention," said Molly.
"Don't be silly," I said.
I mean, how could an attitude adjuster possibly backfire?
I couldn't wait to get started on my new invention.
I also couldn't wait to fix Oliver's bad attitude.
He was complaining about everything.
"You should have an elevator in your building,"
he said as we climbed the stairs to my apartment after the shoe store.
"Or at least an escalator," he added.
"Oliver is driving me crazy!" I thought.
"Whoever heard of an escalator in an apartment building?"
"Why are your radiators so loud?"
Oliver asked after we were inside our apartment.
"The heat at my house is really quiet."
Actually Oliver was right about that.
Our radiators were banging and clanking louder than ever.
I figured I'd better start working on my Amazing Attitude Adjuster right away.
But first I had to get Oliver to be quiet.
"Hey, Oliver, do you want to watch TV?" I asked.
"I can turn it on for you."
"Your TV is really small," said Oliver.
"You need a new one."
"You need a new attitude!" I thought.
Even though our TV is small, Oliver finally settled down to watch cartoons.
A few minutes later Molly brought me her toy telephone.
I brought it into my room and started working on my dial-a-joke invention.
At my desk I took out a pencil and a thick pad of paper.
I had thought a lot about the way my invention was going to work.
I'll tell you about that later.
The most important thing was that the jokes had to be funny.
They had to make people laugh so they would get a better attitude.
If someone had a really bad attitude, though, she or he might need a lot of jokes.
I decided I would need at least one-hundred jokes for Oliver.
This was not going to be easy!
I went into my brother's room.
He was listening to music with his earphones.
"Tate!" I yelled loudly so he would hear me.
"Do you know any more jokes?"
"What?" yelled Tate.
I yelled louder.
"I said, do you know any more jokes?"
Tate took out his earphones.
"I know a great joke," he said.
"What did the big fish do to his pesky little brother?"
"What?" I asked.
Tate grinned. "He told him to go jump in a lake!"
That was Tate's way of telling me to stop bothering him.
But I added Tate's joke to my list anyway.
Oliver was still watching TV.
I went into the kitchen.
My mom was sitting at the kitchen table reading a book.
"Mom, can I knock on apartment doors and ask people for jokes?" I asked.
"Huh?" She looked up from her book in confusion.
I repeated my request.
"Okay," she said slowly.
"But go with Molly, or Josh and Jenny, and stay in our apartment building."
I knew all the neighbors in our building.
But there were only ten apartments, including ours.
We were going to have to work hard to get one-hundred jokes.
Well, ninety-nine, if you counted Tate's.
I heard Oliver's TV show end.
Then Oliver shouted, "I'm bored!
I don't have anything to do!"
I pretended I hadn't heard him.
I opened the door and raced out of the apartment as fast as I could.
I hated to admit it, but Tate was right.
Being a big brother was much harder than being a little one.
Luckily, my Amazing Attitude Adjuster was going to fix that.
It was also going to get me into the Inventor's Hall of Fame!
Josh and Jenny weren't home, but Molly came with me to knock on doors.
By lunchtime we had collected 37 jokes.
I wanted to finish my attitude adjuster so I could try it out on Oliver.
I decided 37 jokes was enough for now.
That night I worked on my new invention while Oliver was asleep.
I couldn't wait to try it out on him!
Suddenly the radiators in our apartment started banging more loudly.
Boom! A really loud bang came.
I ran into the kitchen.
My mom and Tate came running out of their rooms too.
"What happened?" I cried.
"I don't know," said my mom.
"The radiators were banging very loudly," I said.
"But they're quiet now."
Mom turned on the water in the kitchen sink.
"There's no hot water," she said.
"The furnace that heats the building must be broken.
That means it's going to get pretty cold in here soon."
She turned to me.
"Get some extra blankets from the front closet, Iggy.
And please get some for Oliver too."
I couldn't believe Oliver had slept through all the banging.
He was still sleeping when I got back to my room.
I threw some blankets over him, and then jumped into bed to get warm.
"Boy," I thought before I fell asleep.
"Oliver is really going to start complaining when he wakes up!"
The next morning the apartment felt even colder.
I waited to hear Oliver say something about how miserable it was.
He stretched and sat up in bed.
"Hey, it's cold in here!" he said.
"It sure is," I thought.
In my room it was like the North Pole!
"We don't have any heat or hot water," I told him.
"The furnace broke."
It was a good thing my Amazing Attitude Adjuster was all ready.
I was going to need it!
I waited for Oliver to start yelling.
But to my surprise, he brightened up.
"Wow!" said Oliver, "we're like pioneers living in the Old West."
"But it's really cold," I said, shivering.
"And we don't have fur coats like pioneers."
Still Oliver didn't complain.
He was cheerful as we put on our coats and mittens to have breakfast.
"This is fun!" said Oliver.
"Nothing exciting like this ever happens at my house."
Mom smiled at him.
"You have a great attitude, Oliver," she said.
I looked at Oliver and frowned.
For some reason his good attitude was putting me in a bad mood.
"The building superintendent said the furnace will be fixed in two days," my mom said.
"Two days?" I blurted out.
"We have to live without heat and hot water for two whole days?"
"That sounds great to me!" said Oliver.
"We can heat up our water over the fire like Pioneer Pete."
Pioneer Pete is a character from a TV show for little kids.
I used to watch the show all the time.
My mom laughed.
"The stove still works, so we don't need a fire to heat our water," she said.
"But that's a good idea, Oliver."
Molly, Josh, and Jenny came over after breakfast.
They all thought it was an adventure having no heat or hot water.
Even Tate was in a good mood.
"At least the computer still works," he said.
"I'll build a fire," said my mom.
"We can toast marshmallows tonight."
"Yay!" cheered Oliver.
I scowled. What was Oliver so happy about anyway?
Being cold was no fun.
Besides, if everyone was happy, no one would need my Amazing Attitude Adjuster.
My brilliant invention would be a big waste!
My mood got worse as the day went on.
Molly, Josh, Jenny and I huddled in front of the fire.
Meanwhile Oliver was skipping and singing around the apartment.
"My hands are cold and so are my feet.
You can call me Pioneer Pete!"
I put my hands over my ears.
"Will you stop making so much noise, Oliver?"
Oliver stopped. He looked surprised.
"Iggy," Mom said sharply. "Oliver was just having fun."
Everyone stared silently at me.
I could tell they agreed with my mom.
"Well, having no heat is no fun," I complained.
"And now no one needs my Amazing Attitude Adjuster.
Maybe I should just throw it away!"
"What's an Amazing Attitude Adjuster?" asked Jenny.
"It's my new invention.
It helps people get a good attitude," I said.
"Maybe we should try it on you," said Molly.
"Yeah!" Josh added. "Just to see if it works, I mean."
I stared at them.
Were my friends saying I had a bad attitude?
"Come on, Iggy," Molly coaxed me. "It'll be fun."
"Okay," I finally agreed.
"But I didn't invent it for my own attitude."
In my room I showed Josh how to use the attitude adjuster.
Then we brought Molly's telephone and pad of paper into the living room.
Josh handed Oliver a scarf.
"Blindfold Iggy so he can't see anything."
Giggling, Oliver stood on the couch and tied the scarf around my head.
"Now Iggy will dial a telephone number on Molly's telephone," Josh said.
"Jenny, you write down the number Iggy dials."
After I dialed, Oliver took off my blindfold.
Then Josh added up the numbers I had dialed.
"Twenty-eight," said Josh.
"Molly, turn to page 28 in the joke pad and read the joke out loud."
Molly flipped to page 28 and began to read.
"Why did the skeleton go to the party alone?"
"Why?" I asked.
"Because he had no body to go with!" said Molly.
Everyone laughed, even me!
We took turns using the Amazing Attitude Adjuster all afternoon.
The more we played, the better I felt.
We had so much fun that the day flew by.
We were startled when a knock came at the door.
It was Uncle John and Aunt Julia.
They were back from their cruise.
"Guess what?" Oliver ran to his parents.
"What?" Aunt Julia hugged him.
"My shoes got burned, and the furnace broke," said Oliver.
"It was so much fun!"
Uncle John laughed and looked at Aunt Julia in amazement.
"I can't believe it!"
Oliver nodded. "We got our attitudes adjusted too.
I can't wait to come back to Iggy's apartment again!"
After Oliver left, I got my invention ready for the Inventor's Hall of Fame.
First I had to take a picture of it.
Then I had to write down how it worked.
My mom helped me mail everything to the Hall of Fame.
If my invention was good enough, it would be included in the Hall of Fame forever!
Two weeks later I got a letter back.
I sat down next to the radiator in our kitchen and tore it open.
Our furnace was fixed now, and the warm radiator was making cozy hissing noises.
"Dear Iggy," the letter read. "Your Amazing Attitude Adjuster is amazing!
Your invention has earned an honorable mention in the Hall of Fame."
"Mom?" I asked. "What does 'honorable mention' mean?"
"It means that your invention earned special praise," she answered. "Congratulations!"
So I got an honorable mention.
But I did not make it into the Inventors' Hall of Fame.
Not yet anyway.
Just wait until you see what I'm going to invent next!
I sat in my fourth-grade classroom, doodling with a pencil.
Our teacher, Mrs. Romano, was writing on the whiteboard.
She was teaching us how to solve word problems with answers in the millions.
I couldn't see the whiteboard too well though.
Molly's headband was in the way.
She had decorated it with a huge pink flower from the Dollar Delight store.
The flower had fallen off twice that morning, but Molly kept putting it back on.
Now it bobbed in front of me.
"Remember, class, we have a math test one week from today," said Mrs. Romano.
A few kids groaned, but I just went back to doodling.
I wasn't worried about the math test.
I'm pretty good at math.
I can easily add up numbers in the millions.
In fact, I can even add up numbers in the billions!
"If only I could think of a million new inventions," I thought.
"But lately I can't even think of one."
My cousin Oliver had visited this past winter.
During his visit I had invented The Amazing Attitude Adjustor.
It worked great.
But now it was spring, and I had not thought up one single new invention since Oliver left!
I was getting pretty worried about it.
"Don't worry, Iggy,"
Molly had said last week on the way to school.
"You're just going through a fallow time."
"What's a fallow time?" I asked.
Molly shrugged. "I have no idea.
But sometimes my dad has trouble thinking up new ideas at work.
Whenever that happens, he says he's going through a fallow time."
Soon our math lesson was over.
"Class, please come to the rug," said Mrs. Romano.
"We have time to read one more chapter in our science fiction story."
As we all walked over to the rug, Molly's flower fell off her headband again.
Evan accidentally stepped on it.
"Hey, watch out for my flower!" said Molly, picking it up.
"It's the only one I have."
"Why don't you plant it?" joked Colby.
"Then you'll have a whole garden of flowers!"
"Fake flowers don't grow in gardens, silly," said Molly.
Mrs. Romano sat in her chair and opened the book we'd been reading this month.
It was a cool story about aliens landing on Earth.
They get lost in a zoo and have adventures with all the animals.
"Oh dear." Mrs. Romano glanced around.
"I think I misplaced my glasses again."
"I'll help you look for them," said Jake, jumping up.
Everyone joined in the search.
We looked on Mrs. Romano's desk and under her chair.
"I always lose my glasses." Mrs. Romano sighed.
"I wish someone would invent a way to find lost glasses."
Finally Ruby found Mrs. Romano's glasses on the bookshelf, right behind Mrs. Romano's chair.
Mrs. Romano put them on.
"It's so hard to find lost glasses," she said.
"Because when you aren't wearing your glasses, you can't see anything!"
I glanced at the big pink flower on Molly's headband.
At that moment something amazing happened.
An idea for a new invention popped into my head.
It was one of the best inventions I had ever thought of!
While Mrs. Romano read to us, I kept thinking about my new idea.
I couldn't wait to tell Molly about it.
"Molly!" I said when we lined up after recess.
"I'm not having a fallow time anymore.
I got an idea for a fantastic new invention!"
Molly grinned and gave me a high five.
"That's great!" she said. "Iggy the incredible inventor is back!"
"What's your new invention, Iggy?" asked Molly.
"It's something to help people find their glasses," I explained.
"Mrs. Romano will love it!" said Molly.
"There's just one thing," I went on.
"What?" asked Molly as we got in line for the bumpy slide on the playground.
The slide was new, and everyone at our school was really excited about it.
They were so excited, in fact, that the line was always very long.
It was hard to wait for your turn sometimes.
"I need to borrow your flower for my invention," I told Molly.
She put her hand up to her headband.
"My beautiful pink flower?"
"I promise I'll give it back," I said.
"I just want to see if my idea works."
"I have to think about it," said Molly.
"How long do you need to think?" I asked.
"I have to think about that too," said Molly.
I shook my head.
She had to think about thinking about it?
Just then a boy behind us bumped into Molly, and her flower fell off again.
"No pushing in line!" called Mr. Dalmati, the recess helper.
Molly picked up her flower.
"I'm sorry," said the boy. "I didn't mean to push.
I'm just really excited about going down the bumpy slide."
By the end of recess, Molly and I had gone down the slide only once.
"I like the slide," I said, "but I miss running around the playground and playing games."
"I wish we could stand in line and run around at the same time," said Molly.
"Me too," I said.
After recess Mrs. Romano told us she had a surprise.
"Next week a special person is coming to visit our school," she announced.
"His name is Mr. Bright, and he is an inventor."
"I bet he gets lots of bright ideas!" Evan joked. All
of the kids laughed. "Just
like Iggy!" added Molly. "He's an inventor too." "That's
right," said Mrs. Romano, smiling at me. "But
this time I want everyone to be thinking of ideas for inventions. Mr.
Bright will choose the best one to include in his new book, The Kids' Invention Guide ."
Jake moaned. "But how do we think up an invention, Mrs. Romano?" he asked.
Mrs. Romano smiled.
"Just look for a way to solve an everyday problem.
Problems are everywhere, right under your nose!"
I leaned forward to whisper to Molly.
"So can I borrow your flower?
I'm going to need it."
Molly turned around.
"I'm still thinking about it, Iggy!"
That afternoon Molly, Jenny, Josh, and I walked home from school together.
The air was warm, and the trees were beginning to turn green.
Jenny was sad.
Sara, her best friend in third grade, was moving away.
"I'm going to miss Sara," said Jenny.
"We wear matching sweaters and matching shoes all the time.
We even have matching glasses."
"Is Sara moving far away?" asked Molly.
"She's only moving ten blocks away," said Jenny.
"But she'll be going to a different school now.
We both cried when we said good-bye."
"You'll be able to visit her," I said.
Jenny nodded. Then I told Jenny and Josh about Mr. Bright's visit.
The kids in Josh's class were writing down their ideas for inventions too.
"I have a great idea for a new invention," I said, looking at Molly.
"If someone will let me borrow her pink flower."
"I've been thinking,"
said Molly as we approached a lady walking a little dog on a leash.
"And I decided—"
Molly never finished her sentence.
Just then Jenny tripped over the dog's leash.
Then Jenny went flying through the air!

episodes.title: Jenny Takes a Fall—and That's Not All!

subtitle.text: Jenny landed on the sidewalk with a thud.
The lady's little dog barked and barked.
"Oh dear! Are you all right?" cried the lady.
Josh helped Jenny stand up.
Her knee was skinned, and she looked stunned.
"I'm okay," she said, brushing herself off.
"I guess I just didn't see the dog's leash."
Once I was sure that Jenny was all right, I looked at Molly again.
"So can I borrow your flower?"
This time Molly nodded.
"I made up my mind," she said.
"You can borrow it."
"Wow, thanks!" I said.
"I promise to take good care of it."
When we got to Molly's apartment, she took the flower off her headband.
Then she handed it to me.
"I'm going home right now to try my new invention on my mom!" I said.
"Good luck!" called Molly as I ran across the hall to my apartment.
At home my brother, Tate, was using the computer.
My mom was in the kitchen, making meatloaf for dinner.
"Guess what, Mom," I said.
"I have an idea for a great new invention!"
"Uh-oh," said Tate, looking up from the computer.
"He's going to make a big mess."
My mom winked at me.
"That's wonderful, Iggy," she said.
"Can I borrow your reading glasses?" I asked.
"They're on the kitchen table," my mom replied.
"Please be careful with them though.
I can't read a thing without them."
I took Molly's flower and my mom's glasses into my room.
Carefully, I unwound the wire stem of the flower.
Then I wrapped it around the frames of my mom's glasses.
The pink flower stood up, bright and tall.
My mom would never lose her reading glasses with that flower attached to them!
Then I realized something.
My mom never loses her reading glasses anyway.
She always puts them on the kitchen table.
How was I going to test out my new invention if my mom never lost her glasses?
That was a problem I could solve.
After all, Mrs. Romano had said that inventors are problem solvers, right?
"Iggy!" my mom called, "I need my glasses for a minute.
I have to check something in my cookbook!"
"Okay, Mom," I said, walking into the kitchen.
"But first you have to find your glasses."
"What are you talking about?" asked my mom.
"You just took them into your room."
"I know," I said, "but now I'm going to hide them."
My mom looked puzzled.
"Is this some kind of game?"
"No," I said.
"But I want to test my new Fabulous Glasses-Finder invention.
And I can't test it unless you lose your glasses."
"That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard," called Tate from the living room.
"Well, okay," said my mom.
"But I don't have much time.
I'm in the middle of preparing dinner."
I grinned. "It won't take long," I said.
"The Fabulous Glasses-Finder is my best invention yet."
"Don't believe him, Mom!" said Tate.
"You're never going to see your glasses again!"
I told my mom to cover her eyes.
Then I hid her glasses on a chair in her bedroom.
That's the kind of place where someone might leave their glasses by mistake.
"Okay, Mom!" I said, "You can start looking now!"
It took my mom only three minutes to find her glasses.
It was very easy to spot them with Molly's pink flower sticking up.
My mom picked up her glasses and looked curiously at the flower.
"Well," she said. "I must say, Iggy.
This is a very clever idea."
"Did you hear that, Tate?" I shouted.
"My Fabulous Glasses-Finder really works!"
The next morning in school I told Mrs. Romano about my new invention.
Then I showed her Molly's pink flower.
"Why, Iggy," she said. "What a marvelous idea!"
"Can I put the flower on your glasses?" I asked.
Mrs. Romano nodded so I wrapped the wire stem around the frames of her glasses.
When she put the glasses on, everyone started laughing.
"Mrs. Romano, you look funny with a flower sticking up from your glasses!" cried Evan.
"Well, at least I won't lose them," said Mrs. Romano, smiling.
But when Mrs. Romano went to feed the goldfish, the flower fell off her glasses.
It tumbled right into the fish tank!
Lauren scooped it out.
"Iggy!" cried Molly.
"You promised to take care of my flower.
You didn't tell me it was going to get wet!"
"I'm sorry," I said.
"I didn't think it would fall into the fish tank."
We put the flower on a sunny windowsill during art class so it would dry.
When we came back from art, Mrs. Romano suggested that someone else try the Fabulous Glasses-Finder.
"Let me try it!" said Kristin.
That's when things really started to go wrong.
First the flower fell over Kristin's eyes and she couldn't see.
She bumped into a desk and nearly fell over.
Then the wire stem kept sticking her in the head.
"Ouch," said Kristin, rubbing her head.
"This thing hurts."
Soon Kristin got tired of wearing the flower on her glasses.
Lauren said she would wear it next.
I attached the flower to Lauren's glasses at recess.
She was in line for the slide when she leaned over to tie her shoe.
That's when the flower stem got caught on Ruby's sweater.
"Help! We're stuck together!"
cried Ruby, trying to step away.
